title: IELTS Academic Reading Test 2
description: A full 40-question academic reading exam covering urban farming, solar energy, and animal migration.

passage.title: The Rise of Urban Farming
passage.subtitle: How cities around the world are transforming rooftops and vacant lots into productive green spaces

paragraphs.text: Urban farming — the practice of cultivating, processing, and distributing food in or around urban areas — has gained remarkable momentum over the past two decades. Once considered a fringe movement, it is now embraced by city planners, environmental advocates, and entrepreneurs alike. From rooftop gardens in New York to vertical farms in Singapore, urban agriculture is reshaping the way metropolitan populations think about food production.

The motivations behind urban farming are as diverse as its practitioners. Food security is a primary driver, particularly in cities where access to fresh produce is limited by geography or income. Community gardens in low-income neighbourhoods have been shown to improve nutrition outcomes, reduce food expenditure, and foster social cohesion among residents who might otherwise have little interaction with one another.

Environmental benefits also play a significant role. Transporting food across continents contributes substantially to greenhouse gas emissions, and growing produce locally can dramatically cut these so-called food miles. Moreover, urban green spaces act as carbon sinks, absorb stormwater, and reduce the heat-island effect that makes cities significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas.

Despite these advantages, urban farming faces considerable challenges. Land in cities is expensive and often contaminated with heavy metals or other pollutants from decades of industrial use. Securing funding, navigating zoning regulations, and attracting consistent volunteer labour are ongoing struggles for many community-led projects. Critics also point out that urban farms typically cannot match the output of conventional industrial agriculture and therefore cannot serve as a complete substitute.

Technology is beginning to address some of these limitations. Hydroponic and aeroponic systems allow crops to be grown without soil, using up to 95% less water than traditional farming. LED lighting has made indoor vertical farms viable even in basements or windowless warehouses. Sensors and automation reduce the need for manual labour, making it possible to manage large growing areas with minimal staff.

Governments in several countries have begun to formalise their support for urban agriculture. In France, a law passed in 2018 requires new commercial rooftops above a certain size to be either greened or fitted with solar panels, directly encouraging urban food production. Japan's Ministry of Agriculture actively subsidises rooftop farms in Tokyo, viewing them as part of a broader national food resilience strategy.

The commercial viability of urban farming remains debated. Some high-profile ventures have collapsed under the weight of high operational costs and thin profit margins. Others, however, have found success by targeting premium markets, partnering with local restaurants, or integrating farming with leisure and education. The lesson, many practitioners argue, is that urban farming must be adapted to its local context rather than applied as a universal template.

passage.title: Solar Energy: Beyond the Panel
passage.subtitle: Innovations in photovoltaic technology are opening new frontiers for renewable power generation

paragraphs.text: For most of its commercial history, solar energy has been synonymous with the flat, blue-black photovoltaic panels mounted on rooftops or arranged in open-field arrays. This image, however, is rapidly becoming outdated. A new generation of solar technologies is embedding electricity generation into buildings, vehicles, clothing, and even roads, promising to turn virtually any surface into a potential power source.

Building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) represent one of the most commercially advanced of these innovations. Unlike conventional panels, which are bolted onto existing structures, BIPV products are designed as structural components — solar roof tiles, transparent window glazing, or facades that replace conventional cladding. Tesla's Solar Roof, launched in 2016, brought BIPV to mainstream consumer attention, though its high installation cost has limited widespread adoption.

Floating solar farms — panels installed on reservoirs, lakes, and other bodies of water — offer a different set of advantages. They avoid competition with agriculture or urban development for land use, while the water beneath the panels keeps them cooler, improving efficiency by as much as 10 to 15 percent. Several Asian countries, including China, Japan, and South Korea, have invested heavily in floating solar infrastructure, with China now hosting the world's largest such installation.

Perovskite solar cells have attracted enormous scientific interest in recent years. These materials, named after the mineral with the same crystal structure, can be manufactured at low cost using relatively simple printing processes. In laboratory conditions, perovskite cells have achieved efficiency rates comparable to conventional silicon cells. The main obstacle to commercialisation is durability: perovskite cells currently degrade significantly faster than silicon alternatives when exposed to moisture and heat.

Solar-powered transportation is another frontier. Commercial solar-assisted aircraft, boats, and experimental road vehicles have all demonstrated the technology's viability for mobility applications. More practically, solar charging infrastructure is spreading rapidly: parking canopies fitted with photovoltaic panels can generate electricity while simultaneously providing shade for vehicles, offering a dual-use solution that is particularly attractive in hot, sunny climates.

Despite the excitement surrounding these developments, significant barriers remain. The intermittency of solar power — the fact that panels produce electricity only when sunlight is available — continues to pose challenges for grid stability. Battery storage technology has improved dramatically but remains expensive. Grid integration, smart energy management, and demand-side flexibility are all necessary complements to expanded solar capacity if the technology is to fulfil its potential as a primary energy source.

passage.title: The Navigational Mysteries of Animal Migration
passage.subtitle: Scientists are uncovering the remarkable biological mechanisms that guide animals across vast distances

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.heading: An ancient puzzle
paragraphs.text: Every year, billions of animals undertake journeys of extraordinary length and precision. Arctic terns fly from pole to pole and back again — a round trip of some 70,000 kilometres. Monarch butterflies navigate from Canada to a specific forest in Mexico, a journey of up to 4,500 kilometres, accomplished by individuals that have never made the trip before. Humpback whales cross entire ocean basins with a geographical accuracy that rivals modern GPS systems. How these animals navigate has fascinated and puzzled scientists for centuries.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.heading: The role of the magnetic field
paragraphs.text: One of the most compelling explanations involves the Earth's magnetic field. A growing body of evidence suggests that many migratory species possess a form of magnetoreception — the ability to detect magnetic fields and use them as a compass. In birds, researchers have identified cryptochrome proteins in the eye that may interact with the planet's magnetic field through quantum mechanical processes. Sea turtles appear to use both the intensity and inclination of the field to determine their position, allowing them to return to the exact beach where they hatched decades earlier.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.heading: Celestial cues and landmarks
paragraphs.text: The magnetic sense is rarely the only tool at an animal's disposal. Many species also use celestial cues — the position of the sun, the pattern of stars, or the plane of polarised light — to orient themselves. Migratory songbirds have been shown to calibrate their magnetic compass using the rotation of the night sky around the celestial north pole during their first autumn. Landmarks, both visual and olfactory, supplement these celestial and magnetic systems, particularly during the final stages of a journey when precision becomes paramount.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.heading: Inherited maps and individual learning
paragraphs.text: A long-standing question in migration science concerns how much of navigational ability is innate and how much is learned. Research on first-year migratory birds, which in many species travel independently of adults, suggests that a genetic programme provides a basic vector — a direction and approximate distance. This programme, however, is not infinitely precise, and young animals gradually refine their routes through experience. In species such as whooping cranes, juveniles that migrate alongside experienced adults develop superior navigational skills, demonstrating the importance of social learning.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.heading: Chemical signposts
paragraphs.text: Olfaction — the sense of smell — plays a larger role in navigation than was historically appreciated. Pacific salmon are perhaps the best-studied example: they imprint on the unique chemical signature of the stream in which they hatched and use this olfactory memory to locate it precisely when returning years later to spawn. Recent research has also suggested that some seabirds use odour maps of the ocean surface, detecting gradients of compounds such as dimethyl sulphide to orient themselves far from any visible landmarks.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.heading: Threats to migratory pathways
paragraphs.text: Human activity is disrupting migratory systems in multiple ways. Light pollution interferes with the celestial orientation of birds and insects; some species are fatally attracted to artificial lights, colliding with buildings in their millions each year. Noise pollution — particularly from shipping and sonar — disrupts the acoustic cues used by whales and dolphins. Climate change is altering the timing of seasonal events, creating mismatches between the arrival of migratory species and the peak availability of the food resources they depend upon.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.heading: Conservation and future research
paragraphs.text: Protecting migratory species requires international cooperation, since their journeys frequently cross political boundaries. Conservation efforts increasingly focus on safeguarding entire flyways and migration corridors rather than isolated habitats. Advances in miniaturised tracking technology — satellite tags light enough for small birds to carry — are enabling scientists to map routes in unprecedented detail, revealing bottlenecks, stopovers, and critical resting sites that warrant protection. Understanding how animals navigate is not merely an academic exercise; it has direct implications for the survival of some of the planet's most remarkable creatures.
